source.title: How to inject knowledge efficiently? Knowledge Infusion Scaling Law for Pre-training Large Language Models
source.authors: Kangtao Lv; Haibin Chen; Yujin Yuan; Langming Liu; Shilei Liu; Yong-Wei Wang; Wen-Bo Su; Bo Zheng

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor PDF-to-text layout issues in equations and tables.
record.tranche_reason: The authors use the general idea of scaling-law prediction, explicitly drawing inspiration from Chinchilla, to predict knowledge-infusion quantities. Their experiments measure knowledge memorization under infusion, not the held-out pretraining loss, loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on memorization rate and optimal knowledge-infusion frequency. These are related to scaling but are not the held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal parameter/token split named in V1–V7. Its cited language-model scaling results are not its own results.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the Chinchilla-style power-law form (F(C)=A/C^α+E) to fit its own law for optimal knowledge-infusion frequency. Its measures are memorization rate on injected Wikidata facts (multiple-choice perplexity ranking) and fitted infusion-frequency optima. It reports no held-out pretraining loss, no loss extrapolation, no compute-optimal parameter/token split, no architecture-shape effect on loss, and no fitted downstream-vs-scale law. Its statement that memorization rises monotonically with model size is qualitative. It concerns a deliberately injected-fact construct, so it does not bear on V6 as stated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that larger models reach the collapse point at lower infusion frequencies. They claim optimal infusion scales super-linearly with training tokens, and that their law lets small-model experiments predict optimal infusion for larger models.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies the frequency of infused facts and measures memorization rate, then fits a law for optimal infusion frequency. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or optimize parameter/token allocation for fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with model size, training-token budget, infusion frequency, and knowledge-template diversity.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted optimal infusion frequency at 58B tokens falls from 58.2 (137M) to 35.4 (3B). At 75B and 100B the maxima are higher (about 112–159) but not monotone in model size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimal frequency of injected-fact repetition depends on model size and token budget.

fits_no_version.finding: The Chinchilla-style power law of optimal frequency across model sizes fits with R²=0.9685 (P3). Alternative curve forms give 0.60–0.90.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The knowledge-infusion scaling law fits collapse points across 137M–3B models, and the fit quality depends on the chosen curve form.

fits_no_version.finding: Template diversity (1/10/100 templates) changes memorization by at most about 4 points for 377M and 562M models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Template diversity has small effects on injected-fact memorization at these sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: The text states memorization improves monotonically with model size at identical frequency, and with training tokens. This is not given as a number in any row.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Injected-fact memorization improves with model size and token budget.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The experiments are limited to models up to 3B parameters. The authors note that exact surface-form filtering cannot eliminate interference from semantically equivalent paraphrases. Several numerical outcomes are available only as figure labels or plotted curves; no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 2 and Figures 3 and 6 show memorization-rate curves across injection frequencies, but most individual curve-point values are not stated numerically; they are not transcribed as separate rows. Figure 7's template-comparison curves are also not numerically itemized beyond the values in Table 13.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss law is extrapolated from small runs; only infusion-frequency optima are extrapolated.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; token budgets are fixed at 58B/75B/100B.
Depth and width co-vary with size; there is no fixed-parameter shape comparison.
No loss power law in other modalities or regimes.
Memorization of injected facts is reported to rise with size and tokens, but only qualitatively. No predictive downstream fit is given.
There is no comparison of loss-law exponents across fitting choices. The P1–P5 comparison concerns the memorization curve form.

record.verdict_notes: Cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as inspiration for the functional form. The 'collapse' is induced by deliberate over-repetition of injected facts. All optima are read from figure labels. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss power laws fitted on small runs predict loss for much larger runs.
The loss-minimising parameter and token allocation for fixed compute.
The effect of architecture details on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Whether the claimed loss power law holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream-task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of the claimed loss-law exponents or compute-optimal split on fitting and setup choices.
